\section{Experiments}\label{sec:exp}

This section presents the experimental evaluation on HRSID and a cross-dataset transfer to PSeg-SSDD. We first describe the dataset, the training protocol, and the seed discipline. We then report the progressive main results, compare with published state-of-the-art methods, and present two controlled ablations: the fusion operator and the architecture side. We next analyze the two optional trained tiers, the boundary-patch refiner and the learned re-ranker, each with its own leakage audit, and examine qualitative results on representative scenes, first against our own base and then against two detectors that we trained ourselves on the same split. We then transfer the complete recipe to PSeg-SSDD, compare it there against six methods that we trained ourselves under one protocol, and apply the identical recipe to six frozen carriers spanning five architecture families in order to test whether any of it depends on our own base. Finally, we re-read the same predictions as a detection-level false-alarm and missed-detection accounting and verify the robustness of the recovery gain across seeds.

\subsection{Dataset and Protocol}\label{sec:exp:setup}

\textbf{Dataset and splits.} All experiments were conducted on HRSID, evaluated as SAR ship instance segmentation; every number in this section is COCO mask AP $\times$100, reported to one decimal. The dataset comprises 5604 SAR chips of $800\times800$ pixels with instance-level mask annotations, split into 3642 training and 1962 test images. Following the inshore/offshore protocol of prior work \cite{o2former2025}, the official test set is additionally partitioned into an inshore subset of 369 images and an offshore subset of 1593 images. We report all three splits throughout: the official split has no published competitor row and is given for completeness, whereas the inshore split is where the open problem lives.

\textbf{Training protocol.} The base model, denoted c0, is a standard Mask2Former (M2F) \cite{mask2former2022} with a ResNet-50 backbone and 100 queries, initialized from COCO instance-segmentation weights. It was fine-tuned at $800\times800$ with AdamW at an initial learning rate of $2.5\times10^{-5}$ with step decay, batch size 2 with 2-step gradient accumulation (effective batch 4), for 100\,872 iterations; at two images per iteration this amounts to 201\,744 image passes over the 3642-image training split, i.e., 55 epochs. Training ran on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090\,Ti. No layer, loss, or schedule of the base was modified.

\textbf{Seed discipline and evaluation.} All base-level claims use three independent seeds (s0/s2/s3); the inter-seed standard deviation of the base is approximately $\pm$0.3 AP, and single-seed differences within this band are treated as noise. The weight soup is a deterministic single checkpoint (the elementwise average of the three seeds), and the TTA evaluation is deterministic inference, so every stack-level figure is reproducible from fixed artifacts. All of our configurations were scored against the identical official ground truth with the identical COCO evaluator; every within-article delta is therefore a same-GT, same-protocol comparison. Competitor numbers in Section~\ref{sec:exp:sota} are taken from their published tables and were not re-evaluated by us; the attendant caveats are stated there.

\subsection{Main Results}\label{sec:exp:main}

Table~\ref{tab:main} and Fig.~\ref{fig:progression} report the progressive recovery stack. Each row adds one operator to the previous row. No row retrains or modifies the base. The weight soup lifts the three-seed base from 27.7/45.6/59.6 to 29.6/47.4/61.1 inshore/official/offshore at unchanged $1\times$ inference; six-view multi-scale flip-TTA raises the inshore split to 36.1; widening to eight views over $\{640,800,960,1088\}\times\{\mathrm{identity},\mathrm{flip}\}$ yields 37.1/52.6/64.2 under box-NMS; and replacing box-NMS with the consensus-vote fusion of Section~\ref{sec:fusion} completes the full method at \textbf{38.8/53.8/64.8}. The composed lift over the base is +11.1/+8.2/+5.2, a relative inshore gain of +40\%, at zero additional training and roughly $8\times$ inference.

The first two operators compose near-additively. Soup alone contributes +1.9 inshore and the six-view TTA alone +6.9, predicting 36.5 where the measured combination is 36.1, a $-0.4$ sub-additive interaction; we explicitly do not claim synergy. The fusion operator then contributes +1.7/+1.2/+0.6 over box-NMS on the identical candidate set; Section~\ref{sec:exp:fusion} shows this term is an enabler rather than a third additive gain. On the full-metric axis, the stack moves inshore AP$_{50}$ from 61.8 to 75.6 (+13.8), inshore AP$_{75}$ from 22.1 to 36.1 (+14.0), and inshore AP$_s$ from 24.3 to 35.8, so detection, strict-overlap quality, and small-target coverage all participate in the recovery. As a control, a three-model prediction ensemble over the same eight views reaches 39.3/53.6/64.0 at $3\times$ model cost against 38.8/53.8/64.8 for the soup-based method at $1\times$, confirming that the weight soup captures the seed diversity of a full prediction ensemble at one third of its inference cost \cite{modelsoups2022}.

Two results in Table~\ref{tab:sota_in} carry the comparison. With both optional tiers, inshore reaches 44.5 AP, 48.3 AP$_{75}$, and 42.0 AP$_s$, leading every published method in all three columns by +1.4, +2.4, and +2.1 over O2Former, the strongest of them, which reports 43.1, 45.9, and 39.9. That margin costs 55 epochs plus a 19-minute post-processor and a 19-second re-ranker, against 500 epochs of specialized training. The refiner alone already reads 43.6/47.0/41.4 and leads the same three columns, so the leadership does not hinge on the re-ranking tier. The training-free stack alone already posts an inshore AP$_{50}$ of 75.6, exceeding O2Former's 69.5 by +6.1, although it does not lead on absolute inshore AP (38.8 against 43.1) and its AP$_{75}$ of 36.1 trails their 45.9: the stack is a detection-and-recall recovery, not a boundary-precision method. Offshore, the complete pipeline trails the two strongest specialized methods (70.1 against 71.7 and 70.9), with the training-free stack further behind on that split. Even there, our offshore AP$_{50}$ of 98.6 is the highest in Table~\ref{tab:sota_off}, and the near-shore split, where the open problem lives, is where the proposed pipeline leads every published method on AP, AP$_{75}$, and AP$_s$ simultaneously. No competitor reports the official split; our figures there (59.4 with both tiers, 53.8 training-free, 45.6 base) are provided for future comparison.

One caveat dominates all others and we state it plainly: the two columns of results are not at the same operating point. The competitor protocol trains segmentation heads from scratch for 500 epochs on an ImageNet backbone, whereas we fine-tune a COCO-initialized model for 55 epochs. The same Mask2Former architecture scores 17.9 inshore under their protocol and 27.7 under ours, a 9.8-point separation before any contribution of this article. Absolute AP across the two regimes is therefore not directly comparable. This is mainly because the pretraining regime, not the architecture, sets the baseline level, which is itself a central finding of Section~\ref{sec:exp:arch}. The defensible claims are the training-free recovery (+11.1/+8.2/+5.2 on a strong base at zero extra training) and the two audited micro-tiers stacked on top of it, a band-guarded boundary correction (Section~\ref{sec:exp:bpr}) and a mask-preserving re-ranking (Section~\ref{sec:exp:rerank}). Together they spend a deliberation budget where the competitor protocol spends a training budget.

\subsection{Fusion Operator Ablation}\label{sec:exp:fusion}

All operators in Table~\ref{tab:fusion} consume the identical soup $\times$ wide-8-view candidate set; only the merge rule changes. Fig.~\ref{fig:fusion} visualizes the outcome. It can be observed from Table~\ref{tab:fusion} that the fuser, not the view count, decides whether aggressive TTA helps or harms.

\begin{table}[!t]
\caption{Fusion Operators on Identical Soup $\times$ 8-View Candidates (Mask AP $\times$100)}
\label{tab:fusion}
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
Fusion operator & Inshore & Official & Offshore \\
\midrule
box-NMS (reference) & 37.1 & 52.6 & 64.2 \\
matrix-NMS & 4.1 & 8.9 & 14.4 \\
majority pixel vote & \textbf{39.1} & 48.7 & 55.9 \\
probability mean & \textbf{39.1} & 48.7 & 55.9 \\
seed vote & 38.2 & 53.5 & \textbf{64.8} \\
\textbf{consensus vote} ($S_{\max}=6$) & 38.8 & \textbf{53.8} & \textbf{64.8} \\
\bottomrule
\multicolumn{4}{l}{\footnotesize Bold denotes the best value in each column.}
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[!t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figs/fig3_fusion}
\caption{Fusion-operator ablation on identical 8-view candidates (Table~\ref{tab:fusion}). Bar shade encodes the split, darkest inshore to lightest offshore. Matrix-NMS, in the dotted region, collapses to 4.1/8.9/14.4; majority voting erodes the offshore split to 55.9, below the dotted 59.6 no-TTA base; the consensus vote, in the solid region, matches or exceeds the seed vote on all three splits. The probability-mean control is not drawn as a sixth group because it reproduces the majority column bitwise (39.1/48.7/55.9).}
\label{fig:fusion}
\end{figure}

Each failure has a distinct mechanism. Box-NMS suppresses in box-IoU space, and berthed parallel hulls share high box IoU while their masks barely overlap; hard deletion therefore removes true inshore neighbors, capping the reference at 37.1. Matrix-NMS is the collapse mode: its soft score decay deletes nothing, so with eight views each object arrives roughly eight times and the decayed near-duplicates flood the top-100 ranking, driving AP to 4.1/8.9/14.4. Majority pixel voting is the strongest inshore reading at 39.1 but erodes offshore to 55.9, below the 59.6 no-TTA base: multi-scale views misalign by one to two pixels along long hull boundaries, and unconditional pixelwise voting trims every disputed pixel. The probability-mean control replaces binary voting with floating-point averaging before thresholding and reproduces the majority result bitwise (39.1/48.7/55.9); the erosion therefore stems from cross-view misalignment, not from binarization loss, and the correct degree of freedom is which mask to keep, not how to average pixels. The seed vote keeps each cluster's highest-scoring mask verbatim: it never erodes (offshore 64.8) and beats box-NMS on all three splits (+1.1/+0.9/+0.6), but concedes inshore at 38.2 by forgoing denoising entirely.

The consensus vote resolves this trade-off by gating on cross-view agreement: clusters with support in the band $2\le|C|\le S_{\max}$ are majority-denoised, all others emit their seed mask verbatim. It matches or exceeds the seed vote on every split (38.8/53.8/64.8; inshore AP$_{75}$ 36.1 against 35.3 for the seed vote) and behaves monotonically in the band ceiling: $S_{\max}=4/5/6$ yields inshore 38.4/38.6/38.8 with offshore pinned at 64.8 throughout.

\subsection{Architecture-Side Controlled Study}\label{sec:exp:arch}

We frame this study as the regime experiment: on the same strong COCO-initialized base, we attempted seven architecture- and training-side directions under matched protocol, hunting for any modification worth its complexity. Table~\ref{tab:arch} and Fig.~\ref{fig:arch} record the outcome: all seven were flat, negative, or insufficient, which we report as controlled evidence for the regime diagnosis, under the same seed discipline as the positive results.

\midrule

\begin{figure}[!t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figs/fig4_arch}
\caption{Inshore mask-AP deltas of the architecture- and training-side probes (Table~\ref{tab:arch}). The upper group is measured against the c0 base (27.7) and the lower group against the full method (38.8); a hollow marker on the zero line denotes a flat direction. No probe reaches the training-free recovery, whose $+$11.1 runs off this scale and is drawn as the arrow at the top.}
\label{fig:arch}
\end{figure}

The mechanisms differ by direction. OffsetAdj constrains the sampling offsets of the multi-scale deformable attention and costs $-$1.0 inshore: the sampling geometry is exactly what COCO pretraining has already tuned, and constraining it perturbs the alignment. CHART, a one-to-many auxiliary supervision on the decoder, collapsed validation AP to 0.18 at auxiliary weight 1.0 and was flat at 0.1. CAST, a hard-sample paste augmentation, was flat at 27.7, absorbed by the strong baseline, as were all four training-side families (capacity, feature enrichment, data augmentation, supervision). A MaskIoU rescoring head is worth +1.5 inshore and +1.7 official standalone at its $\lambda=0.2$ operating point, yet leaves a +0.1 residual under the stack: the weight soup subsumes its gain. The SGA strip adapter deserves emphasis because it preserves the COCO initialization exactly: sequential $1\times7/7\times1$ depthwise strip convolutions, consistent with the sequential-decomposition guidance of \cite{striprcnn2026}, sit behind a scalar zero-initialized residual gate \cite{cait2021}, so the model starts fine-tuning as the identical COCO network. It still lost 0.9 inshore while gaining 0.6 offshore: the elongation prior fits large well-resolved offshore hulls and mismatches the quasi point-like inshore targets. Preservation alone does not rescue a mismatched prior.

The backbone swap is the most instructive arm. Swin-S carries a +3.2 COCO mask-AP advantage over ResNet-50 (46.1 against 42.9), which shrinks to +0.9 inshore on SAR (28.6 against 27.7), the only positive base-level delta in the sweep. Under the recovery stack (single seed, no soup) it reaches 37.3/52.5/63.5, below the ResNet-50 full method on all three splits. COCO backbone rankings do not transfer to this domain, and the base-level margin does not survive the pipeline.

The equal-epoch control asks whether the gap to 500-epoch competitors is a schedule artifact. We extended training to 200 epochs: the validation trajectory ran 43.5, 44.8, 44.9, saturating near epoch 45, and an early-decayed warm restart reached a best official base of 46.4, a +0.8 gain over the 55-epoch 45.6 that concentrates in AP$_{75}$ (51.5 against 49.4). With the recovery stack applied (single seed; a soup at $3\times200$ epochs is unaffordable), the 200-epoch model reaches 37.9/52.5/63.5, below the 55-epoch three-seed configuration at 38.8/53.8/64.8. Longer training does not close the inshore gap: the marginal base gain neither survives the stack nor compensates for the missing soup.

\subsection{Boundary Refinement Analysis}\label{sec:exp:bpr}

The stack's residual error is boundary quality. Mask logits are predicted at stride 4 ($200\times200$) and bilinearly upsampled $4\times$ to $800\times800$, so predicted contours carry a soft halo of roughly one to two pixels; on a typical $9\times18$-pixel inshore hull, a one-pixel boundary shift costs roughly 0.15--0.25 IoU. No training-free operator we tested moves this residual: binarization-threshold, probability-averaging, interpolation, and radiometric re-ranking controls were null or negative. We therefore added the optional trained tier of Section~\ref{sec:bpr}: a boundary-patch refiner in the BPR paradigm \cite{bpr2021}, a 2.35M-parameter UNet trained once, in about 19 minutes, on (prediction, ground-truth) boundary patches harvested from the training split, and applied under a $\pm$4-pixel band guard that leaves every out-of-band pixel and every detection score untouched.

\caption{Mask AP$_{50}$ and AP$_{75}$ before and after boundary-patch refinement (Table~\ref{tab:bpr}); each pair runs from the training-free full stack to the refined result. The strict-overlap gains of +10.9/+8.4/+5.7 on the inshore/official/offshore splits, set against AP$_{50}$ pairs that barely separate, are the fingerprint of a pure boundary correction.}
\label{fig:bpr}
\end{figure}

Table~\ref{tab:bpr} and Fig.~\ref{fig:bpr} quantify the effect. The refiner adds +4.8/+4.7/+4.4 AP and +10.9/+8.4/+5.7 AP$_{75}$ on inshore/official/offshore, respectively (deltas computed from unrounded values). The metric fingerprint is exactly that of a boundary correction: inshore AP$_{50}$ moves by only +0.7 (75.6 to 76.3) while inshore AP$_{75}$ moves by +10.9 (36.1 to 47.0). Detection and recall composition are untouched. The gain concentrates entirely at strict IoU, its magnitude matches the halo arithmetic above (a one-to-two-pixel correction is precisely the band in which instances cross the 0.75 threshold), and inshore AP$_s$ rises from 35.8 to 41.4, confirming that the correction lands on the small near-shore hulls the diagnosis targeted.

A post-processor trained on (prediction, ground-truth) pairs invites the suspicion that test ground truth leaks into the output, so we audited the application path along seven attack vectors; all are clean. (1) No ground-truth access: the apply path receives no annotations, and the refined result regenerates MD5-identically from predictions, refiner weights, and images alone. (2) Band confinement: in 90 of 90 sampled instances, zero edited pixels fall outside the $\pm$4-pixel band. (3) Score integrity: 0 of the roughly 237\,000 detection scores change. (4) Determinism: an independent re-run reproduces every reported AP to four decimals. (5) Visual evidence: refined contours track image scattering evidence, and false-positive masks are also edited toward that evidence, which would be impossible if the refiner copied ground truth, since false positives have none. (6) Split hygiene: the filename overlap between refiner training patches and test images is zero. (7) Metric fingerprint: the +0.7 AP$_{50}$ versus +10.9 AP$_{75}$ signature excludes any mechanism that adds, removes, or re-scores detections. One honesty note remains: the inshore row, on which the headline claim rests, received the full audit; the official and offshore rows were verified by the same band- and score-integrity spot checks rather than an exhaustive per-instance re-derivation.

\subsection{Learned Re-Ranking Analysis}\label{sec:exp:rerank}

The stack and the refiner leave a third residual, and it is not in the masks. It is in the order the masks are ranked in. Mask2Former scores an instance as the product of its classification confidence and the mean foreground confidence of its mask, a quantity that never compares that mask with the object it covers, so a tight hull and a loose one at equal class confidence are ranked alike; average precision is an integral over a ranking, so a re-ordering alone moves it. Section~\ref{sec:rerank} specifies the operator that exploits this. A gradient-boosted regression tree ensemble over the 14 scalars of Eq.~(\ref{eq:rrfeat}), six of which the consensus fusion has already computed, is fitted on the pipeline's own training-split candidates against their mask IoU with the annotation and blended into the score by Eq.~(\ref{eq:rrblend}), at a weight chosen on 728 held-out training images. It reads no image pixel and it fits in 19 seconds on CPU. This subsection reports what it buys, what it costs on the columns it does not help, and whether it can be cheating.

\label{tab:rerank}

Table~\ref{tab:rerank} reports the effect on top of the refined stack. Re-ordering alone is worth +1.0/+0.8/+1.0 AP inshore/official/offshore (+0.97/+0.82/+0.95 before rounding), +1.3/+0.7/+0.6 AP$_{75}$, and +0.6/+0.6/+0.7 AP$_s$, at +0.4/+0.1/+0.1 AP$_{50}$. Nothing is added, removed, or reshaped: the same detections match the same annotations at the same IoU levels, and only their position in the score-descending list changes, which is why the movement is small, positive at every threshold, and evenly spread rather than concentrated at strict overlap the way the boundary correction was. One column moves the other way and we report it plainly. Large-object AP falls by 1.4, 1.3, and 1.3 points on the three splits (48.3 to 47.0 inshore). The regressor is fitted on all training candidates, which are overwhelmingly small vessels, and it demotes a few of the rare large instances in exchange for promoting many small ones; on HRSID that trade is strongly net positive, and on a large-vessel-dominated corpus it would need to be re-examined.

A component trained on prediction and ground-truth pairs and then applied to test predictions invites the same suspicion the refiner did, so we audited it along six vectors; all are clean. (1) No leakage: the regressor is fitted only on training-split predictions and training-split annotations, the apply path receives no test annotation of any kind, and every feature it consumes is computable from the prediction alone. (2) Masks untouched: not one mask byte changes, the run-length encodings and the cardinality of the candidate set are identical to the refined input, and only the score field is rewritten; detections that find no match in the stack dump keep their original score, which is 4682 of 28\,539 inshore, 55\,348 of 118\,922 official, and 50\,666 of 90\,383 offshore. (3) Determinism: an independent re-run regenerates the output files byte-identically and reproduces every reported AP. (4) Predictive validity: on held-out training images the predicted mask IoU tracks the realized one at a Spearman rank correlation of 0.68 (Section~\ref{sec:rerank}), so the component ranks by mask quality rather than by a memorized identity. (5) One model, no per-split tuning: a single regressor with a single $\alpha$ is applied unchanged to all three splits, and $\alpha$ itself was chosen on held-out training images, never on test. (6) Resampling: across 1000 bootstrap resamples of the inshore test images the gain is positive in 100\% of them, with a 95\% confidence interval of [+0.61, +1.23].

Columns show, from left to right, the SAR image with ground truth, Mask R-CNN, Cascade Mask R-CNN, the training-free stack, the stack with the boundary-patch refiner, and the same with the learned re-ranker. Two variants on the same axis returned nothing, and both are informative. The first is a miss-rescue verifier: a small convolutional network re-scores the rejected tail of the candidate pool, those detections scoring in $[0.01, 0.35)$, and appends whatever it endorses at a capped score below the kept floor. It rescued 9402 inshore, 10\,145 official, and 743 offshore detections and moved AP to 43.5/58.5/69.1 against 43.6/58.6/69.1, a null within three hundredths of a point and marginally negative; stacked on the re-ranker it repeats the null. The mechanism is that our dumps already run down to score zero at 100 detections per image, so a ship the pipeline has seen at all is already somewhere in the ranked list. There is no missing detection to rescue, only a badly placed one to promote, which is what the re-ranker does. The second variant extends the feature vector from 14 to 16 with two depth-consistency descriptors, the mean mask IoU of the seed instance across the last three decoder layers and its score trajectory across them, on the hypothesis that an instance stable across decoder depth deserves trust. It ties: 44.5/59.3/70.0 against 44.5/59.4/70.1. Stability across decoder depth and agreement across views carry the same information on this data, because the late decoder layers converge on exactly the instances the views already agree about, so the two extra columns are redundant with the six consensus features that are there. We report both nulls because the axis they failed on is the axis the re-ranker succeeded on, and the contrast is the evidence that ranking, not recall, was the residual.

\subsection{Qualitative Analysis}\label{sec:exp:qual}

Fig.~\ref{fig:qual} traces where the recovered AP lives at instance level, on four test scenes ordered by target density. The dense harbor of row (a) holds 88 annotated ships; the base finds 31 of them while raising 37 false alarms and missing 57. The training-free stack lifts the same scene to 72 true positives, 28 false alarms, and 16 misses: 41 of the 57 missed targets are recovered while false alarms drop from 37 to 28. Movement in both directions at once is the fingerprint of view-consensus filtering; a lowered decision threshold would buy recall with additional false alarms, whereas mask-level voting across the six views admits the dim, consistently re-detected hulls and suppresses the view-unstable clutter responses. The quay line of row (b) repeats the pattern at smaller scale, from 17/19/7 (TP/FP/FN) at the base to 23/12/1 under the stack, and the refiner clears the final miss to 24 of 24; the parallel-berthed group of row (c) goes from 5 of 7 to 7 of 7. In the offshore scene of row (d), all three configurations detect all 5 ships with no false alarms, consistent with the near-saturated offshore AP$_{50}$ of Table~\ref{tab:bpr}; what remains there is boundary quality, and the inset magnifies the true positive whose mask the refiner edits most, trimming a loose stern boundary (the stack mask and its refined version agree at only 0.685 IoU on that hull).

The failure modes are equally visible. Residual red contours in rows (a)--(c) sit almost exclusively on bright quay structures and unlabeled lookalike clutter, the same radiometrically ambiguous responses that survive consensus because they persist across views; at the 0.3 display threshold the stack still reports 28, 12, and 5 false alarms in the three inshore scenes (one of them, in row (c), a duplicate fragment inside the largest ship that persists across the prediction columns at this display threshold). The refiner itself changes counts only at the margin, as its band guard promises: in row (b) one borderline hull crosses the 0.5 matching threshold upward (23 to 24 true positives), while in row (a) one crosses it downward (72 to 71), a reminder that a pure boundary edit can move an instance across a fixed matching threshold in either direction while the AP gains of Table~\ref{tab:bpr} accrue at strict IoU.

\subsection{Comparison With Independently Trained Detectors}\label{sec:exp:qualcmp}

Section~\ref{sec:exp:sota} compares against published HRSID figures produced under a different protocol, and Section~\ref{sec:exp:qual} compares the pipeline against its own base. Neither puts the pipeline and a competing detector on the same scene at the same budget, so Fig.~\ref{fig:qual-hrsid-multi} does that on three HRSID test scenes: inshore chips \texttt{P0115\_4800\_5600\_9600\_10400} with 95 annotated ships and \texttt{P0111\_5400\_6200\_9600\_10400} with 88, and offshore chip \texttt{P0072\_1200\_2000\_5400\_6200} with 5. The 88-ship chip of row (b) is a different scene from the 88-ship harbor of Fig.~\ref{fig:qual}(a). Scene selection is programmatic and reproducible: the two inshore scenes maximize one point per recovered target plus half a point per removed false alarm against the better of the two competitors on that same scene, subject to at least 8 annotated ships and at most five false alarms above that competitor, and the offshore scene is, among the 20 scenes that clear a filter requiring at least five annotated ships and zero misses and zero false alarms from every method, the one with the largest cross-method spread in mean mask IoU. The Mask R-CNN and Cascade Mask R-CNN columns are our own trainings on the identical 3642-image training split, for the identical 55 epochs, scored by the identical evaluator; they are two of the three HRSID carriers of Table~\ref{tab:univ}, whose carrier-alone inshore AP reads 28.3 and 30.4. A third detector trained under that same protocol, SOLOv2, is the weakest of the three and is omitted from the figure for width: it reads 19.0 inshore, 38.2 official, and 54.0 offshore mask AP, with an inshore AP$_{75}$ of 15.7 against 24.8 and 27.0 for the two columns shown, and it is carried through the same three-rung ladder in Table~\ref{tab:univ}. On the 95-ship chip of row (a) the two competitors find 23 and 28 of the annotated ships while raising 32 and 44 false alarms, and the training-free stack finds 66 at 34. On the 88-ship chip of row (b) they find 25 and 34 at 29 and 33 false alarms, and the stack finds 65 at 35. The complete per-panel accounting, in the column order Mask R-CNN / Cascade Mask R-CNN / Ours / Ours$+$BPR / Ours$+$BPR$+$re-ranking, reads 23/32/72, 28/44/67, 66/34/29, 65/35/30, and 65/35/30 true positives, false alarms, and missed targets on row (a) and 25/29/63, 34/33/54, 65/35/23, 65/35/23, and 65/35/23 on row (b), with mean matched mask IoU of 0.692/0.703/0.704/0.768/0.770 and 0.696/0.703/0.734/0.788/0.786, respectively. The false-alarm column barely moves across that transition, 32 and 44 against 34 and 35, so between 1.9 and 2.9 times as many targets are found at a comparable false-alarm count. That arithmetic is the signature of recall recovery rather than of a lowered decision threshold, which would have raised both columns together, and it is the same recall-and-precision-together behavior that Section~\ref{sec:exp:qual} reported against our own base, now measured against detectors trained under our protocol rather than against an earlier rung of our own pipeline.

The two trained tiers then act where the counts have stopped moving. In row (a) the refiner and the re-ranker hold 65 true positives against the stack's 66, one instance crossing the 0.5 matching threshold downward, while the mean mask IoU of the matched instances rises from 0.704 to 0.768 and then 0.770; in row (b) all three of our columns read 65/35/23 and the mean matched IoU rises from 0.734 to 0.788, with the re-ranker at 0.786. Flat counts with rising overlap are the instance-level form of the AP$_{50}$-flat, AP$_{75}$-up pattern that Tables~\ref{tab:bpr} and~\ref{tab:rerank} report. Row (c) removes detection from the comparison altogether: all five method columns find all 5 offshore ships with no false alarms, so boundary quality is the only quantity left, and it separates them at 0.782 and 0.777 for the two competitors against 0.828 for the stack and 0.873 for both trained tiers, a cross-method spread of 0.263 on the hull the inset magnifies. One caveat travels with the figure. The competitor columns are trained at our budget and not at theirs, so what is shown is a same-protocol comparison and not a statement about the published systems of Table~\ref{tab:sota_in}, whose 500-epoch scratch rows score higher in absolute terms than the carriers plotted here.

\subsection{Cross-Dataset Generalization}\label{sec:exp:ssdd}

The recipe transfers to PSeg-SSDD with one proportional change. We retrained only the base under the protocol of Section~\ref{sec:exp:setup}: three seeds (s0/s2/s3) of the identical COCO-initialized Mask2Former, 8352 iterations each at an effective batch of 4, that is, 36 epochs over the 928-image official training split, averaged into a weight soup; the 232-image test set is partitioned into 46 inshore and 186 offshore scenes following \cite{o2former2025}. The wide-TTA scale set is rescaled in proportion to the smaller native chips, from $\{640,800,960,1088\}$ to $\{416,512,608,704\}$; the consensus band $2\le|C|\le S_{\max}=6$ is carried over unchanged; the boundary-patch refiner is retrained for 20 epochs on patches harvested from SSDD training-split predictions, with the $\pm$4-pixel band guard unchanged; and the re-ranker is refitted on SSDD training-split predictions from the identical 14 features, with its blend weight re-selected by the same held-out sweep, which returns $\alpha=1.0$ here, so the SSDD re-ranker replaces the score outright instead of blending it. Table~\ref{tab:ssdd} reports the outcome. The soup base scores 60.9/51.9/64.8 mask AP on the official/inshore/offshore splits; the training-free stack lifts it to 63.3/54.0/66.9, the refiner to 66.3/60.0/68.8, and the re-ranker to 67.5/62.1/69.8, a composed lift of +6.6/+10.2/+5.0 (stack +2.4/+2.1/+2.1, refiner +3.0/+6.1/+1.8, re-ranking +1.2/+2.1/+1.1; deltas computed from unrounded values). Every operator keeps the sign it had on HRSID. The refiner again concentrates at strict overlap, raising inshore AP$_{75}$ from 54.9 to 72.5 and official-split AP$_{75}$ to 82.9, and the re-ranker carries those two figures to 74.6 and 84.9. A fusion-ordering probe also replicates: majority pixel voting reads 56.9 on the SSDD inshore split against 54.0 for both the consensus and seed votes, the same inshore lead it shows on HRSID, and we retain the consensus operator because the offshore-erosion cost of unconditional voting was established there (Section~\ref{sec:exp:fusion}).

The transfer also fixes the position of the method against specialized architectures on this dataset. Under the same split protocol, the complete pipeline exceeds the from-scratch Mask2Former baseline tabulated by O2Former (52.5 inshore, 67.2 offshore) by +9.6/+2.6, and closes to 1.1 inshore and 2.1 offshore points below the 500-epoch specialized architecture itself (63.2/71.9) \cite{o2former2025}; the near-shore gap that stood at 3.2 points after the refiner is 1.1 after re-ranking. The magnitude of each tier tracks regime difficulty. SSDD single-view predictions are more stable than their HRSID counterparts (base inshore 51.9 against 27.7), so the variance-driven stack has less to remove: its inshore lift is +2.1 here against +11.1 on HRSID. The boundary tier moves in the opposite direction and dominates the SSDD composition, contributing +6.1 of the +10.2 inshore lift and +17.6 inshore AP$_{75}$. Fig.~\ref{fig:qual-ssdd} traces the same behavior at instance level, now against the competing architectures rather than against our own tiers. In the inshore harbor of row (a), Mask R-CNN, CondInst and M2F$+$OAEM find 7, 5 and 6 of the 10 annotated ships while the full method finds all 10; the recall is bought with false alarms, 12 against the 7 of M2F$+$OAEM, the recall-for-consensus trade of Section~\ref{sec:exp:qual} at smaller chip scale. Row (b) is the sharper case: on 13 ships along a quay the two conventional detectors collapse to 4 and 3 true positives, M2F$+$OAEM reaches 11 with 5 false alarms, and the full method reaches 13 with the same 5 false alarms, so the recall gain there is free. Row (c) isolates the boundary tier: all five methods detect all 7 offshore ships with no false alarms, and only mask quality separates them, with mean IoU against ground truth of 0.888, 0.836, 0.859, 0.867 and 0.898 in column order. The refiner therefore also wins the scene in which detection is already saturated, and the inset magnifies the hull on which the five columns disagree most. The complete per-panel accounting, in the column order Mask R-CNN / CondInst / M2F$+$OAEM / Ours / Ours$+$BPR, reads 7/7/3, 5/0/5, 6/7/4, 10/12/0, and 10/12/0 true positives, false alarms, and missed targets on row (a), 4/4/9, 3/3/10, 11/5/2, 13/5/0, and 13/5/0 on row (b), and 7/0/0 for every method on row (c); the M2F$+$OAEM column is our own reimplementation of that module on our carrier and not the published O2Former system. Scene selection is again programmatic: the two inshore scenes maximize the missed-target gap against the strongest competitor, M2F$+$OAEM, subject to at least 8 annotated ships, and the offshore scene is the one detected in full by every method with the highest Ours$+$BPR mask IoU.

\input{tab_fafn}

Because PSeg-SSDD is small enough to retrain competitors on our own hardware, we complement the relayed literature numbers of the preceding paragraph with a comparison in which every row is ours. Table~\ref{tab:ssdd_cmp} reports six independently trained methods spanning four families: a two-stage region-based detector and its deformable-convolution variant, a single-stage prototype detector, a single-stage dynamic-kernel detector, and two SAR-specific modules grafted onto the same Mask2Former carrier that our own base uses. Neither of those two modules has public code, so both were reimplemented by us from their published descriptions; the rows report our reimplementation on our carrier and not the published systems, and they are labeled accordingly in the table. The training-free full method exceeds all six on all three splits, and with both trained tiers the inshore margin over the strongest of them, our OAEM reimplementation at 53.2, is +8.9, while the official and offshore margins are +6.7 over M2F $+$ OAEM (60.8) and +4.7 over Mask R-CNN (65.1). The ranking inside the competitor block is itself informative. The four generic architectures cluster between 38.9 and 41.2 inshore, a spread of 2.3 points across two-stage, prototype, and dynamic-kernel designs, whereas the two SAR-specific rows jump to 52.9 and 53.2, so on this dataset the near-shore regime, not the choice of segmentation head, sets the level. Our own unmodified base already reaches 51.9 inshore with no SAR-specific component at all, within 1.3 points of the better of the two specialized rows, and the training-free stack passes both without touching the model.

The two SAR-specific rows carry the most weight in Table~\ref{tab:ssdd_cmp}, because they change the architecture exactly where we do not. As published, OAEM enriches the multi-scale backbone features with an oriented aggregation along the hull axis and a polar position encoding \cite{o2former2025}, and the frequency-domain module of DenoDet V2 soft-thresholds the amplitude spectrum to suppress multiplicative speckle while preserving phase \cite{denodetv22026}. What Table~\ref{tab:ssdd_cmp} measures is our own reimplementation of those two descriptions, written because no code was released for either, and any shortfall against the authors' intent is ours rather than theirs. Both reimplementations sit on the identical COCO-initialized Mask2Former carrier as our base and were trained for the same 36 epochs on the same split. Measured against that shared carrier, they read +1.3 and +1.0 inshore but $-0.1$ and $-0.4$ official and $-0.8$ and $-1.1$ offshore, so each buys a near-shore gain at the price of the other two splits. The training-free stack reads +2.1/+2.4/+2.1 on the same base and keeps the sign on all three. Architectural specialization is therefore not the only way to reach the near-shore regime on this dataset, and in this comparison it is not the more economical one. One selection detail is disclosed rather than corrected: the OAEM and DenoDet checkpoints were selected on the inshore split, which is the split their rows lead, whereas ours follow the best-segmentation-AP convention on the reported split. Both conventions select on the split they report, so the practice is symmetric across rows, but the two specialized inshore entries should still be read as upper bounds.

Fig.~\ref{fig:qual-ssdd8} carries the same eight methods to instance level, and the honest reading of it is narrower than the margins of Table~\ref{tab:ssdd_cmp}. Its three scenes are \texttt{001091.jpg} with 13 annotated ships, \texttt{000219.jpg} with 9, and offshore \texttt{001131.jpg} with 7, the sole offshore scene clearing the same all-methods-complete filter used in Fig.~\ref{fig:qual-hrsid-multi}. The per-panel true-positive, false-alarm, and missed-target counts, in the column order of the figure, read 5/3/8, 4/4/9, 5/3/8, 3/3/10, 9/4/4, 11/5/2, 13/5/0, and 13/5/0 on row (a) and 6/1/3, 7/2/2, 8/4/1, 7/0/2, 9/0/0, 9/1/0, 9/0/0, and 9/0/0 on row (b), while row (c) reads 7/0/0 for all eight methods and separates only on the mean mask IoU of the matched instances, at 0.877, 0.888, 0.878, 0.836, 0.863, 0.859, 0.867, and 0.898. Exactly one of the 46 inshore test scenes yields a strictly positive count gain for our columns over the best of the six competitors on that scene, the 13-ship quay of row (a), where the DenoDet and OAEM reimplementations reach 9 and 11 of the 13 ships and both of our columns reach 13 at the same five false alarms that OAEM already pays. Row (b) is a tie: the two SAR-module columns already find all 9 ships at the 0.3 display threshold, at zero and one false alarm, so our columns can separate only on overlap, at 0.823 and 0.844 mean matched IoU against 0.787 and 0.834. Row (c) is a tie for all eight methods at 7 of 7, with the refined column leading on mean matched IoU at 0.898 against a competitor best of 0.888. We state this rather than select around it, because it is the visible form of what Table~\ref{tab:ssdd_cmp} already reports: on the easier dataset the specialized baselines sit close to detection saturation, and the margin the recipe carries there lives at the mask level and in the ranking, which is where its +6.1 inshore AP and +17.6 inshore AP$_{75}$ from the boundary tier live as well.

\subsection{Universality Across Architectures}\label{sec:exp:univ}

Everything reported so far rides on one carrier, so the recipe could in principle be an artifact of Mask2Former. Table~\ref{tab:univ} settles that question on six further carriers spanning five architecture families across both datasets: a two-stage region-based detector, its cascade variant, a single-stage dynamic-kernel detector, a single-stage prototype detector, and a grid-based mask-kernel segmenter. Each carrier is trained once, frozen, and then handed the identical recipe with no per-carrier tuning of any kind, that is, the same eight views, the same consensus band, the same $\pm$4-pixel band guard, and a boundary refiner fitted by the same script on that carrier's own training-split errors. All 66 cells of the ladder come from re-evaluation, none from transcription. Every one of the 21 endpoints, seven carriers by three splits, improves over its own carrier. On HRSID the two conventional detectors gain +11.9 inshore apiece, from 28.3 to 40.2 for Mask R-CNN and from 30.4 to 42.3 for Cascade R-CNN, and SOLOv2, the weakest carrier in the table at 19.0, gains +14.3 to 33.3; on PSeg-SSDD the three carriers gain +6.9, +16.3, and +6.1. Two intermediate readings are negative and we print them rather than hide them. The training-free rung costs Mask R-CNN 0.6 and YOLACT 0.5 offshore AP on PSeg-SSDD, 65.1 to 64.5 and 63.4 to 62.9, which is the offshore erosion that Section~\ref{sec:exp:fusion} identified for predictions that are already stable on that split, and the boundary tier converts both to +1.4 and +2.7. The single most useful number in the table is 42.3. Cascade R-CNN, an architecture from 2018 with no SAR-specific component and no orientation prior, lands within 0.8 points of the 43.1 that a specialized 500-epoch design reports on the same inshore split, purely by being made to look eight times and correct itself.\footnote{Applying multi-scale flip TTA to Cascade R-CNN first required repairing its mask head. The \texttt{CascadeRoIHead} of mmdetection averages the three stages' mask logits through a routine left over from the removed 2.x augmentation-test interface, which consults the \texttt{flip} flag and tries to un-flip each stage's RoI-local logits. On a flipped view it raises a negative-stride error, and it would be semantically wrong even if it ran, because within one view all three stages already live in that view's frame and the whole-image flip is undone once, after pasting. Our parameter-free override drops the flip handling and is output-identical to the stock head on non-flipped pipelines.} These carriers are our own trainings under our own 55-epoch budget, so their absolute levels are not comparable with the 500-epoch rows of Table~\ref{tab:sota_in}; what transfers across the two tables is the delta, not the level.

The size of the gain is not constant, and its variation is itself a test of the diagnosis. If the recipe removes prediction variance, a carrier with more variance left in it should gain more, and carrier strength is a usable proxy for how much is left. The prediction survives on the total gain, and the paragraph after this one shows that its two tiers reach that total from opposite directions. The two datasets separate accordingly. On HRSID, where every carrier alone sits below 31 inshore AP, the recipe returns between +11.9 and +14.8; on PSeg-SSDD, where the three carriers start between 38.9 and 41.2, two of them return +6.9 and +6.1. CondInst is the exception and we treat it as one. It gains +16.3 inshore, the largest figure in the table, from a carrier-alone 41.2 that sits at the top of the PSeg-SSDD group. Across the seven carriers the Spearman rank correlation between carrier-alone inshore AP and inshore gain is $-0.77$ without CondInst and $-0.11$ with it, so the tendency holds in six carriers and one carrier flattens it to nothing; we report a tendency and not a law. The exception has a mechanism worth naming. The training-free rung alone is worth +8.9 inshore on CondInst against +3.3 and +2.2 on the other two PSeg-SSDD carriers, so its excess gain sits in the variance tier rather than the boundary tier, which is what per-instance kernels generated from a single view's features should do: they are the most view-sensitive readout of the seven, and the consensus vote consequently finds the most to remove.

The three HRSID carriers sharpen this reading, because they hold dataset, split, schedule, and evaluator fixed and vary only the base, and across them the two error axes scale in opposite directions. The detection-variance axis contracts as the base weakens. The training-free stack returns +8.8 inshore on Mask R-CNN and +8.7 on Cascade R-CNN but +6.5 on SOLOv2, and the same ordering holds on the other two splits, +7.4 and +6.8 against +4.8 official and +5.8 and +4.8 against +2.3 offshore. The consensus vote does not invent detections; it promotes candidates the carrier already produces in some views and suppresses in others, so its yield is bounded by the stock of present-but-suppressed candidates the carrier brings into the fusion, and a base at 19.0 inshore AP brings fewer of them than a base at 30.4. The variance tier therefore meets a floor at the weak end, just as Section~\ref{sec:exp:ssdd} found it running out of material at the strong end, where single-view predictions are already stable; it pays most on the intermediate bases that produce the candidates but rank them inconsistently. The boundary axis runs the other way and runs harder. The refiner adds +3.1 and +3.2 inshore on the two region-based carriers against +7.8 on SOLOv2, +4.0 and +4.3 against +10.0 official, and +4.6 and +5.0 against +11.3 offshore, a factor of 2.3 to 2.5 on every split. SOLOv2 forms each mask by convolving one shared feature map with a kernel predicted at a coarse instance grid rather than through a per-region head at RoI resolution, so its silhouettes are the loosest of the three carriers and its carrier-alone inshore AP$_{75}$ is 15.7 against 24.8 and 27.0, which is exactly the state in which a band-guarded refiner has the most to correct. CondInst, the other kernel-generated readout in the table, behaves the same way on the other dataset with the largest PSeg-SSDD boundary gain at +7.4 inshore, so what drives this axis is the mask readout rather than the base level as such; the two travel together here because one coarse readout produces both the weak carrier and the loose contour. The two trends compose instead of canceling. SOLOv2 still returns the largest HRSID total at +14.3 inshore against +11.9 for both region-based carriers, so the tendency of the preceding paragraph survives at the level of the total, but it is the sum of a shrinking variance term and a growing boundary term rather than one monotone effect. This is the most direct evidence in the article that the two axes are distinct quantities and not two readings of one. Orthogonality by itself leaves their dependence on base strength unconstrained, whereas measured here the two dependences carry opposite signs, which no single-axis account of the near-shore residual can produce.

Fig.~\ref{fig:univ-qual} shows what these deltas look like on the image. In the 47-ship HRSID harbor of row (a), Mask R-CNN alone finds 23 targets and misses 24, and the recipe takes it to 38 found and 9 missed at 20 false alarms against 15. The two intermediate rows behave the same way: Cascade R-CNN on the 95-ship HRSID scene of row (b) moves from 28/44/67 to 54/46/41 true positives, false alarms, and missed targets, and CondInst on the 24-ship PSeg-SSDD scene of row (c) from 6/2/18 to 18/2/6. For each carrier the displayed scene is selected programmatically, maximizing one point per recovered target plus half a point per removed false alarm over scenes carrying at least six annotated ships. In the 88-ship scene of row (d) our own carrier moves from 31 found with 37 false alarms to 71 found with 29, recall and precision improving together, which is the signature the consensus vote produced on our own base in Section~\ref{sec:exp:qual} and reproduces here on carriers that share nothing with it except the recipe.

\subsection{Detection-Level Analysis}\label{sec:exp:detect}

Mask AP compresses detection and mask quality into a single number, so Table~\ref{tab:fafn} re-reads the same PSeg-SSDD predictions as Table~\ref{tab:ssdd_cmp} in the terms an operator uses: how many ships are found, how many false alarms come with them, and how the two trade against each other. This accounting and the curves of Fig.~\ref{fig:pr} are computed on the refined predictions, before the learned re-ranking of Section~\ref{sec:exp:rerank}, because the re-ranker rewrites scores and therefore moves what any fixed threshold selects, which would mix a ranking effect into a detection count. Matching is greedy in descending score at mask IoU $\ge 0.5$ with one claim per annotated ship. The table reports both a fixed 0.30 score threshold and each method's own $F_1$-optimal threshold, because that optimum ranges from 0.10 for CondInst to 0.85 for M2F $+$ DenoDet and no single fixed threshold is neutral across that range. Inshore, the refined full method detects 169 of the 172 annotated ships at the fixed threshold ($P_d=0.983$), against 156 and 159 for M2F $+$ OAEM and M2F $+$ DenoDet and between 113 and 127 for the four generic architectures. The recall is not free: it arrives with 1.41 false alarms per image against 1.11 and 1.00 for the two specialized rows, so the fixed-threshold $F_1$ of 0.833 sits below the 0.844 of M2F $+$ DenoDet, and we report the fixed-threshold block as a recall-first operating point rather than as a win. At each method's own optimum the ordering resolves on both summary axes, $P_d^{*}=0.936$ and $F_1^{*}=0.902$ against 0.866 and 0.882 for M2F $+$ OAEM and 0.843 and 0.881 for M2F $+$ DenoDet. Against the generic architectures the comparison is unambiguous at either threshold: the full method finds 168 of 172 inshore ships at 1.44 false alarms per image where Mask R-CNN with deformable convolutions finds 127 at 1.74, more targets and fewer false alarms at the same time.

Offshore, the same accounting is a parity statement and we report it as one. The full method and the two specialized rows all detect 369 of the 374 annotated ships at the fixed threshold, and at their optima all three read $P_d^{*}$ between 0.979 and 0.984 at 0.038 false alarms per image, so the split is saturated and no method has room to separate. Two entries there need an explicit word. The offshore rows of the full method and of its refined version are identical at every swept threshold, which is the expected behavior and not a transcription error: the refiner reshapes boundaries only inside a $\pm4$-pixel band, offshore masks already clear the 0.5 matching threshold by a wide margin, and no instance crosses that threshold in either direction. YOLACT's $P_d^{*}$ of 0.992 is the single best detection rate in the offshore block, but it is reached at a score threshold of 0.15 and at 0.118 false alarms per image, the worst false-alarm figure in that block, which is why $P_d$ and FA/img are printed side by side and why the footnote warns against reading either alone.

Fig.~\ref{fig:pr} plots the same eight methods as precision-recall curves on the inshore split, at the two IoU thresholds that separate the two mechanisms we claim. At IoU $=0.50$, which asks only whether the ship was found, the three rows of our pipeline occupy the top of the panel at 90.8 for the base, 94.3 with the training-free stack, and 95.7 with the refiner, against 92.2 for M2F $+$ OAEM, 92.0 for M2F $+$ DenoDet, and 79.1, 72.1, and 71.1 for CondInst, YOLACT, and Mask R-CNN. The generic architectures run out of recall early: the YOLACT and Mask R-CNN curves reach zero precision before a recall of 0.80 and CondInst before 0.90, whereas the refined pipeline still holds a precision of 0.89 at a recall of 0.90 and 0.84 at 0.95, against 0.76 and 0.45 for M2F $+$ OAEM and 0.84 and 0.56 for M2F $+$ DenoDet, and it is the only one of the eight that reaches full recall at nonzero precision. At IoU $=0.75$ the picture inverts for the training-free tier. The base and the stack read 53.2 and 54.9, below the 55.6 of M2F $+$ OAEM and the 58.8 of M2F $+$ DenoDet, and only the refined row leads, at 72.5. The two panels state the division of labor of the pipeline in one figure: the training-free operators recover detections, the two SAR-specific modules produce slightly tighter masks than our unrefined output, and the boundary refiner is what converts the recovered detections into strict-overlap accuracy.

\subsection{Robustness Across Seeds}\label{sec:exp:robust}

The recovery gain is not a single-seed artifact. Applying the six-view msTTA core to each seed individually lifts inshore AP from 27.7/27.6/27.7 to 34.6/35.0/34.4 for s0/s2/s3, respectively: gains of +6.9/+7.4/+6.7, a mean of +7.0 with $\sigma\approx0.3$, matching the $\pm$0.3 inter-seed noise band of the base itself. The gain also follows the regime gradient, +7.0 inshore against +5.5 official and +3.4 offshore, largest exactly where single-look speckle and dock clutter make single-view predictions most variable. Every artifact above the seed level is deterministic: the soup is a single fixed checkpoint, the TTA and fusion passes are deterministic inference, the refiner re-run reproduces all reported figures to four decimals, and the re-ranker regenerates its outputs byte-identically (Sections~\ref{sec:exp:bpr} and~\ref{sec:exp:rerank}). The recovery framework therefore inherits the seed robustness of its weakest layer, the base training, and adds no stochastic stage of its own.
